sections.h2: Who sets the value on an Ohio tax bill?
sections.html:
Each county auditor appraises the parcels in that county, and your bill starts from the auditor's figure. The state tax department describes a complete reappraisal on a six year cycle. In between, a lighter update every third year leans on sales data instead of a site visit.

A millage rate then turns value into dollars. Inside mills come from local governments without a ballot. Outside mills come from levies voters approved for schools, fire districts and similar services. So a bill can rise even when your house is valued the same, since a fresh levy lifts the rate. The Board of Revision hears disputes over value only. The rate is off the table.

The Department of Taxation property tax page outlines two ways to question the figure. A handful of counties offer an informal review, mostly in reappraisal years. All of them take the formal complaint. Phone the auditor to find out what your parcel qualifies for.

You may settle an Ohio bill in a lump sum or in installments. Under R.C. 323.12, paying everything at once is due by the final day of December. Choosing halves means the first half (plus any older delinquency) is due then, with the balance following on June 20 of the next year. Real bills often show later dates, because R.C. 323.17 moves payment to January 31 and July 20 when the duplicate reaches the treasurer late. Your own bill is the final word on dates.

Money has to reach the treasurer by the deadline, or be mailed with a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated on or before it. Private meter stamps are rejected. Some treasurers hold the books open a short while to process the mail.

The penalty schedule in R.C. 323.121 works like this:

  • Late on the first half: ten percent is added to the unpaid half.
  • Late on the second half: another ten percent lands on whatever current tax is still unpaid.
  • After that, back taxes earn interest at the rate set under section 5703.47.

You begin at the auditor's counter, and the auditor forwards the complaint to the Board of Revision. Under R.C. 5715.19 you have until the later of two dates: the end of March following the tax year at issue, or the day the treasurer wraps up first-half collections. A mailed complaint is judged by its postmark.

Besides the owner, the statute names the owner's spouse, a retained assessment professional, a retained accountant, appraiser or real estate broker, and in some commercial leases the tenant. Bring comparable sales, any independent appraisal you hold, and recent photographs of the house.

You cannot refile within the same interim period unless a new event occurred after the lien date. The qualifying events are:

  • An arm's length sale of the property.
  • A casualty loss of value.
  • A substantial improvement.
  • An occupancy change of fifteen percent or more that hits the property's economics hard.

Still unhappy? The Board of Tax Appeals hears the next round. R.C. 5717.01 sets a thirty day limit that runs from the date the county board mails its notice.

sections.h2: Quick reference for payments and appeals
sections.html:
Ohio property tax payment and valuation rules
TopicWhat the rule says
Standard due datesOne lump sum, or two halves with the second in June
Extended due datesJanuary 31 and July 20 if the duplicate is late
Late penaltyTen percent added to the unpaid half or balance
Tax lienStarts each January 1 and stays until paid
Valuation complaintDue at the auditor by the later of two dates
Appeal of a board decisionBoard of Tax Appeals, thirty days after notice is mailed

A homestead exemption trims the tax on a house you occupy. R.C. 323.152 covers owners who are permanently and totally disabled, owners sixty-five or older, certain surviving spouses, disabled former service members, and the surviving spouses of public service officers killed on duty. Under R.C. 323.151, the protected home includes up to one acre around the dwelling. Anyone who turned sixty-four before January 1 of the application year satisfies the age test.

The basic reduction protects twenty-five thousand dollars of true value, and the tax commissioner adjusts it for inflation. Disabled former service members and surviving spouses of officers killed on duty receive fifty thousand dollars and face no income test. Other applicants must stay under an income ceiling that the statute states as thirty thousand dollars of total income, also indexed each year. Ask the auditor for today's figure.

A second layer applies to any homestead. The statute sets percentages of the tax from qualifying levies. The first tax year the amendment applies earns 5.70 percent, then 8.92 percent, then 12.15 percent, and finally 15.38 percent from the third following year onward. Ask the auditor which step your year falls on.

Applications go to the auditor's office. Most owners use Form DTE 105A, DTE 105I is for disabled former service members and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K is for officers' surviving spouses. Once approved, you remain enrolled until eligibility changes. The owner-occupancy credit is a separate benefit for a primary residence you occupied on the January 1 of the application year.

Each year's tax lien fastens to the land on January 1 and remains until the tax, penalties and interest are cleared, as R.C. 323.11 puts it. A new deed leaves the lien intact. Either the unpaid amount is paid from your sale proceeds or the buyer takes it on. Get a payoff figure from the county treasurer before closing.

The deed step brings one more form. Under R.C. 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value with the auditor, which must say whether the homestead exemption cut your taxes and whether the land was valued for current agricultural use. A buyer who cannot claim a break you enjoyed will see a different next bill.

Owners already behind have an escape route. R.C. 323.31 guarantees an occupant owner a single written delinquent tax contract with the county treasurer. Installments can stretch up to five years, and to at least two if the owner requests it. A missed installment or unpaid current tax voids the deal, and none is available while a tax certificate or foreclosure judgment stands.

Planning a fast sale? Request the treasurer's payoff figure first, then have the title company confirm the lien gets paid from proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can often close quickly enough to clear a delinquency before any foreclosure judgment.

faqs.q: When is the Ohio Board of Revision complaint deadline?
faqs.a: The later of two dates: the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection ends. File with the auditor, who forwards it. A mailed complaint is dated by its postmark.

faqs.q: Can I split my Ohio property tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. You can split the bill into two halves, one near year end and one in June. A late duplicate shifts both into January and July, so rely on the dates printed on your bill.

faqs.q: Can I get a homestead exemption if I am under sixty-five?
faqs.a: Yes, when you are permanently and totally disabled on January 1 of the application year, or when you are a disabled former service member or qualifying surviving spouse. Any homestead also gets a partial exemption. The county auditor takes applications.

faqs.q: Who sets the Ohio millage rate?
faqs.a: Local governments set inside mills, and voters approve outside mills through levies. A valuation complaint cannot change the rate. Only the property's value can be challenged at the Board of Revision.

faqs.q: What if I cannot pay my Ohio property tax on a home I live in?
faqs.a: Ask the county treasurer for a delinquent tax contract. A resident owner is entitled to one, with payments spread over as many as five years. Signing before a foreclosure judgment stops the county from suing while you keep up the installments.
